criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community domestic and multiple-use piped/tap drinking-water supply schemes across three rural communities in South Africa (Tshakuma and Ga-Moela) and Switzerland (Entlebuch, Kanton Luzern).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines collective water governance, municipal co-management, new public management outsourcing, and legal/policy frameworks for rural self-supply. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, despite framing its theoretical critique around modernist and neoliberal imaginaries, the empirical case studies directly analyse rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) collective/cooperative user ownership versus municipal utility ownership and undefined post-handover O&M accountability structures; (2) statutory provider-licensing and public-tendering rules under South Africa's Water Services Act (1997) and Municipal Systems Act (2000) that rendered community-based water providers technically illegal and reliant on municipal discretionary tolerance in a legal grey zone; (3) Swiss spatial planning law (SR 700) assigning self-supply duties to households outside built-up zones alongside cantonal 60% subsidy conditions mandating cooperative mergers and stricter water-quality regulations; and (4) scheme-level cost-recovery rules (mandatory equal upfront financial and labour contributions, monthly operator stipends) and post-construction membership caps that directly determine household inclusion or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative multi-site empirical study using action research, literature/archival review, participant engagement (including a 46-day village stay, 6 community meetings, and 7 planning/focus group meetings in Ga-Moela), and semi-structured interviews with 28 department officials, 12 scheme officials, 9 engineering consultants, 12 politicians, 3 academics, and 64 water users. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal studies with identifiable empirical methods are fully eligible for the systematic review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes directly relevant to household water service access, piped/tap connection, reliability/continuity, breakdown repair response, and exclusion (e.g., 113 connected households with swift repairs vs. excluded households relegated to a weaker collective with erratic service in Tshakuma; frequent pipe leakages, delayed municipal repair materials, shortened lines to tail-end households, and dry taps downstream of the chief's preferential tap in Ga-Moela; recurring breakdowns of aging spring-fed infrastructure serving 14 households in Entlebuch).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (three local water collectives and constituent rural households in Tshakuma, Ga-Moela, and Entlebuch, plus 128 semi-structured interviewees), legal/institutional exposures, qualitative service access/reliability/exclusion outcomes, and qualitative comparative case-study / action-research design are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: We base our analysis on research findings in three case studies of local water commons. The first case study describes user-initiated and constructed schemes situated in Tshakuma, a rural-peri-urban village in Vhembe district in Limpopo province, South Africa.

Community-based initiatives from then on would have to be recognized as water service providers by local government. This was only possible if no government institution could provide these services, and they would have to follow a process of public tendering designed for private service deliverers.

raw_response.exposure: Collective/cooperative user water-scheme ownership and communal management rules (upfront financial/labour contribution requirements, membership caps, vernacular rule enforcement) interacting with statutory, municipal, and regulatory rules (South Africa's Water Services Act 1997 and Municipal Systems Act 2000 provider-recognition and public-tendering mandates, discretionary municipal tolerance of informal schemes, ward-councillor-appointed unpaid volunteer operators; Switzerland's statutory self-supply mandate outside built-up zones, outsourced planning, water-quality regulations, and 60% public subsidy conditions requiring cooperative mergers).
raw_response.outcome: Household and community domestic/multiple-use water access, piped/street-tap connection versus exclusion (exclusion of households unable to afford initial contributions or barred by capacity caps, shortened lines to tail-end households, preferential upstream access), and water service continuity/reliability (frequency of breakdowns/leakages and speed of maintenance response).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Three rural water collectives and their user households across Limpopo Province, South Africa (Muhovhoya scheme serving 113 households in Tshakuma village of >4,000 households; two reticulation collectives in Ga-Moela village of ~100 households) and Entlebuch, Kanton Luzern, Switzerland (cooperative spring-water scheme serving 14 farming/domestic households); interview sample comprises 28 department officials, 12 scheme officials, 9 engineering consultants, 12 politicians, 3 academics, and 64 water users.
raw_response.rationale: This full-text English qualitative action-research and comparative case study satisfies all systematic review inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It empirically investigates household and community domestic/multiple-use water supply schemes in rural South Africa and Switzerland (c1, c3, c5, c6), examining concrete ownership, statutory licensing/tendering rules (WSA 1997, MSA 2000), discretionary municipal accommodation in a legal grey zone, spatial-planning self-supply duties and subsidy-merger conditionalities, and collective upfront contribution and membership-eligibility caps (c2), and reports resulting household connection, exclusion, and service reliability/continuity outcomes (c4). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review regardless of lack of quantitative effect estimates.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative multi-site comparative case study using action research, archival/document review, and semi-structured interviews
